ct-kosta-diamantis-sentenced-2026-09-30.excerpt: Kosta Diamantis was sentenced in absentia for extortion, bribery and false-statement convictions tied to school-construction contracts; federal authorities are still seeking him.
ct-kosta-diamantis-sentenced-2026-09-30.text: former connecticut official sentenced to 7 years after fleeing to greece kosta diamantis was sentenced in absentia for extortion, bribery and false-statement convictions tied to school-construction contracts; federal authorities are still seeking him. former connecticut school-construction official konstantinos “kosta” diamantis was sentenced wednesday to 84 months in federal prison and three years of supervised release, but he was not in the bridgeport courtroom to hear the punishment. the 70-year-old former state official had fled to greece before sentencing, and the u.s. attorney’s office for the district of connecticut said law enforcement is seeking him. the federal announcement is at https://www.justice.gov/usao-ct/pr/former-state-official-sentenced-7-years-federal-prison-school-construction-extortion-and. u.s. district judge stefan r. underhill imposed the sentence for convictions involving extortion, bribery, conspiracy and false statements. a federal jury in bridgeport found diamantis guilty in october 2025 on 21 counts: two counts of extortion, two extortion-conspiracy counts, two bribery counts, two bribery-conspiracy counts and 13 counts of making false statements to federal agents, according to the justice department. connecticut public reported that the case grew out of diamantis’s work as the state’s former deputy budget director and director of the office of school construction grants and review. that office administered grants for connecticut public-school construction projects seeking state funding. prosecutors said diamantis used the position to demand and receive payments from contractors while helping them obtain or preserve work. the justice department identified projects involving a school project in tolland, state reimbursement work for new britain and renovations at hartford’s bulkeley high school. the release says one contractor paid diamantis with cash and checks and hired his daughter at an inflated salary; those details describe the conduct underlying the convictions, not new untested allegations. the sentence came after an unusual break in the normal criminal-justice process. diamantis had been scheduled to appear for sentencing in september but did not attend. ct mirror reported that his lawyer told the court diamantis had left the united states and was in greece, where he holds dual citizenship. the later sentencing could proceed without him, but his absence leaves the practical question of how and when he will be taken into custody. federal officials have not announced that he has returned to the united states. the financial consequences are not settled. the justice department said judge underhill will determine restitution after additional court proceedings. that decision could identify losses that the government says were caused by the scheme, but the sentencing announcement did not give a final restitution amount. the unresolved figure matters because the projects at issue involved public school construction and state reimbursement, placing the case's consequences beyond the contractors and former official who appeared in court. the prison term was also shorter than the range sought by prosecutors. ct mirror reported that the government recommended a guideline range of 121 to 151 months, while the judge imposed 84 months. the difference does not change the convictions or the three-year supervised-release term, but it will be part of the record as prosecutors pursue diamantis and the court addresses restitution. ct mirror’s sentencing report is at https://ctmirror.org/2026/09/30/kosta-diamantis-still-a-fugitive-sentenced-to-84-months/. the case is not finished for the other people involved in the investigation. the justice department said contractors identified as duffy, monarca and roy pleaded guilty to related charges and are awaiting sentencing. the investigation was conducted by the fbi and irs criminal investigation, and federal prosecutors said the bribery scheme involved multimillion-dollar school-construction projects. connecticut public’s account of the sentencing, including the fact that diamantis remained outside the country, is at https://www.ctpublic.org/news/2026-09-30/kosta-diamantis-cts-disgraced-former-deputy-budget-director-sentenced. for connecticut, the public-interest question now extends from the sentence to the systems that allowed a senior official overseeing school-building money to steer contractors while concealing conduct from investigators. the court has established criminal responsibility through the jury’s verdict and the sentence; it has not yet completed restitution proceedings or resolved diamantis’s custody. those next steps will determine how much money is recovered, whether the former official is returned to face the prison term and what accountability reaches the related contractors. new-england new-england new england ct bridgeport bridgeport, ma-college-closure-risk-notice-2026-10-0.excerpt: Higher-education officials are planning an earlier public-warning deadline for financially distressed private colleges after two Massachusetts schools announced plans to close last spring.
ma-college-closure-risk-notice-2026-10-0.text: massachusetts colleges may have to disclose closure risk by dec. 31 higher-education officials are planning an earlier public-warning deadline for financially distressed private colleges after two massachusetts schools announced plans to close last spring. massachusetts higher-education officials are planning to require private colleges and universities judged to be at risk of imminent closure to post a public notice by dec. 31, an effort to give students, employees and surrounding communities more time to respond to a financial crisis. the proposed timing was described by outgoing department of higher education commissioner noe ortega during the board of higher education's sept. 29 meeting, according to wbur and the state house news service (https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/30/massachusetts-private-colleges-higher-ed-closing-risk-schools). the change would not mean that every school posting a notice is certain to shut down. under the state's financial assessment and risk monitoring, or farm, system, an institution is considered at risk of imminent closure when the commissioner determines that it may be unable to continue operations or substantially meet its obligations to enrolled and admitted students through the current and following academic year. the massachusetts department of higher education says the system is intended to identify risks, monitor mitigation plans and reduce disruption to students, families, faculty, staff and host communities (https://www.mass.edu/strategic/farm.asp). the state already requires colleges to alert the board of higher education about known financial liabilities or risks that could lead to an imminent closure or prevent the institution from fulfilling its obligations. the department's farm materials say those immediate notifications are confidential, while public notice is part of a later process if the institution's financial condition remains sufficiently uncertain after review and risk-mitigation planning. the department also requires private institutions to post annual financial reports and plain-language summaries on their websites. the proposed dec. 31 date is meant to make the public-warning process more predictable. wbur reported that current regulations use dec. 1 as the annual threshold measurement date for deciding whether a college can meet its obligations for the rest of the current academic year and the next one, while the board currently has flexibility about when after that date to make a determination. board chairman chris gabrieli said a december determination would reduce the risk that students and staff learn about a potential closure only after they have made plans for the spring semester. the discussion follows two massachusetts closures announced near the end of the last academic year. anna maria college in paxton and hampshire college in amherst cited financial difficulties in announcing plans to close, wbur reported. hampshire's public notice from the department of higher education says the college planned to end academic programming at the end of 2026 while continuing academic programs, residential support and transition services for enrolled students through dec. 31 (https://www.mass.edu/strategic/documents/2026-04-14-hampshire-noitce-posting-for-dhe-website.pdf). the notice also says the department could not confirm that hampshire had enough resources to sustain current operations and fulfill obligations through the current and subsequent academic years; that is a regulatory finding, not a claim that every massachusetts college faces the same condition. massachusetts has been building this oversight system since the sudden 2018 closure of mount ida college. the department says 24 colleges and universities closed, merged or began winding down between 2014 and 2022, and that the 2019 farm law and later regulations were designed to improve financial monitoring and closure planning. those rules can require a contingency plan covering student deposits and records, and in some cases a bond or letter of credit to help protect those obligations. the department's current process describes screening from november through april, review of risk-mitigation plans from june through october, and determinations and contingency planning in november and december. officials also said the board plans to add staff and use outside firms to strengthen financial assessments, while revising required training for private-college trustees. the goal, gabrieli said, is to give students time to identify transfer options, give faculty and staff a reasonable period to seek other work, and reduce the shock to communities that depend on a campus. the timing matters this fall because ortega's term as commissioner ended sept. 30 and josé luis santos began serving as interim commissioner on oct. 1, according to the department (https://www.mass.edu/). the public-warning deadline remains a planned policy change rather than a newly announced closure list. the next questions are whether the board of higher education formally adopts the dec. 31 timetable, which institutions are identified through the annual farm review, and what mitigation or teach-out plans follow. until those steps occur, students should not read the proposed deadline as evidence that a particular college is about to close; it is an attempt to move information earlier when the state does determine that a school's finances may threaten its ability to serve students. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma boston massachusetts massachusetts higher education college closures financial stability department of higher education students

ma-life-sciences-tax-incentives-2026-09-.excerpt: The awards span 38 companies, with most of the expected new positions located outside Boston and Cambridge and commitments subject to three years of reporting.
ma-life-sciences-tax-incentives-2026-09-.text: massachusetts awards nearly $40m in life-science tax incentives tied to 1,644 jobs the awards span 38 companies, with most of the expected new positions located outside boston and cambridge and commitments subject to three years of reporting. massachusetts has awarded nearly $40 million in tax incentives to 38 life-science companies that collectively pledged to create 1,644 new jobs, putting a statewide economic-development program behind expansions in research, therapeutics, diagnostics and manufacturing. gov. maura healey announced the awards sept. 28 at smc ltd. in devens. the figures describe company commitments, not jobs already filled or money paid directly to workers. (https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-40-million-to-grow-massachusetts-life-sciences-industry-create-more-than-1600-jobs) the geographic distribution is a central feature of this round. the massachusetts life sciences center said 31 of the 38 awardees are expanding outside boston and cambridge, and those projects account for 71% of the expected new jobs. that puts communities such as acton, andover, bedford, burlington, chelmsford, devens, framingham, marlborough, milford, northbridge, sudbury, waltham and woburn in the direct path of the announced hiring commitments, rather than limiting the benefit to the state's traditional laboratory hubs. the agency described the program as a way to use massachusetts' broader network of life-science assets for growth and retention. (https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-40-million-to-grow-massachusetts-life-sciences-industry-create-more-than-1600-jobs) the largest individual award goes to acton-based insulet corporation: $10 million tied to a 250-job commitment. lila sciences in cambridge received $3.6 million for 200 jobs, while vertex pharmaceuticals in boston received $3.025 million for 121 jobs. other sizable awards include $2.875 million for bristol myers squibb's 125-job commitment in devens, $1.86 million for transmedics in andover, and $1.35 million for smc's 54 jobs in devens. the boston business journal reported that the full list also includes astrazeneca, vericel, zoll medical, rentschler biopharma and dozens of smaller firms. (https://www.bizjournals.com/boston/news/2026/09/28/mass-tax-incentive-program-2026.html) the awards are tax incentives administered through the massachusetts life sciences center's tax incentive program jointly with the department of revenue. the program is open to companies doing research and development, commercialization or manufacturing in massachusetts, and the commitments are meant to be new, long-term positions. awardees must maintain their job commitments for three years and file regular reports documenting the jobs created as a result of the incentives. that structure makes the announced 1,644 jobs a measurable target that can be checked over time, rather than an immediate headcount. the state release also says the program has supported commitments for more than 22,300 jobs since the center was established. (https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-40-million-to-grow-massachusetts-life-sciences-industry-create-more-than-1600-jobs) demand for the program was stronger than the award total. the boston business journal reported that companies submitted $58 million in applications this year, compared with a previous year when the center needed two rounds to allocate the full $40 million authorization. the outlet also reported that, since 2009, the center has made 519 awards to nearly 300 distinct companies totaling about $422 million and tied to more than 22,300 jobs. those figures show both the scale of the state's strategy and the competitive choices behind this year's list: the program is not an open-ended subsidy for every applicant, and some proposals were not funded in this cycle. (https://www.bizjournals.com/boston/news/2026/09/28/mass-tax-incentive-program-2026.html) the current ceiling comes from the 2024 mass leads act, which raised the annual statutory cap for life-science tax incentives from $30 million to $40 million and broadened the eligible field to include areas such as medical technology, preventative medicine, biosecurity and life-science-related artificial intelligence. massachusetts' technical tax guidance describes the program as a collection of tax incentives available to qualifying companies, rather than a single grant pot. that distinction matters when evaluating the public return: the state is trading foregone tax revenue for promised hiring and investment, while the companies still have to execute their expansion plans. (https://www.mass.gov/technical-information-release/tir-25-5-tax-provisions-in-certain-massachusetts-legislation-enacted-in-2024) for workers and municipalities, the next test is delivery. companies must meet the hiring and retention conditions attached to their awards, and the state must report whether projects translate into sustained employment across the commonwealth. the announcement includes activity in artificial intelligence, women's health, therapeutics, diagnostics, medical technology, research and development and biomanufacturing. if the commitments hold, the round will distribute new positions across a wider geography and reinforce massachusetts' life-science supply chain; if projects fall short, the reporting and tax-administration process will determine how the state responds. the award announcement establishes the targets, but future compliance records will show how many jobs actually materialize. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma massachusetts massachusetts life sciences tax incentives jobs economic development biotechnology

ma-public-benefit-fraud-auditor-report-2.excerpt: A new state report says investigators identified fraudulent overpayments in 402 cases from January through June, while agencies had finalized $285,339 in civil recoveries and restitution settlements.
ma-public-benefit-fraud-auditor-report-2.text: massachusetts auditor identifies $10.6m in public-benefit fraud, reports limited recoveries a new state report says investigators identified fraudulent overpayments in 402 cases from january through june, while agencies had finalized $285,339 in civil recoveries and restitution settlements. massachusetts state auditor diana dizoglio's office said wednesday that its bureau of special investigations identified $10.6 million in public-benefit fraud during the first six months of 2026, a finding that puts new numbers around losses in programs used for health care, food assistance and family support. the report covers january 1 through june 30 and is based on investigations completed by the bureau, not on criminal convictions in every case. (https://www.mass.gov/news/auditor-dizoglios-bureau-of-special-investigations-identifies-over-106-million-in-public-benefit-fraud) the bureau investigated 2,223 cases during the period and calculated overpayments in 402 cases where it identified fraud, according to the state auditor's report. masshealth and medicaid accounted for the largest share: $6,051,185, or 57% of the total. the supplemental nutrition assistance program accounted for another $3,854,119, or 36.3%. personal care attendant services represented $538,332, followed by $130,483 in transitional aid to families with dependent children and $38,463 in emergency aid to the elderly, disabled, and children. the categories add up to $10,612,582. the distribution matters because the reported losses touch programs with different administrators and different kinds of eligibility records. masshealth helps pay for medical care, snap helps eligible households buy food, and cash-assistance programs support families or people facing emergencies. a finding of an improper payment does not by itself establish who caused it or whether a criminal case will follow; the report describes the bureau's investigative findings and overpayment calculations, while other agencies handle enforcement and collection. the pace of identified fraud was higher than in the preceding six-month reporting period. boston 25 news, reviewing the new report, said the auditor's office had identified about $4.4 million in the prior period. the station also reported that the latest total included two dental providers accused of billing masshealth for “impossible days,” including days when their offices were closed. the report does not name suspected fraudsters, and the figures should be read as a snapshot of cases completed during the reporting period rather than a complete measure of all improper payments in massachusetts. (https://cmg-cmg-tv-10020-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/news/local/25-investigates-106m-benefits-fraud-little-clawed-back/tdd6wuwflre3xau536qiw6ac5a/) the state's recovery figures are much smaller than the amount identified. the report lists $285,339 in restitution settlements and civil recoveries for the two quarters combined, roughly 2.7% of the $10.6 million identified. that comparison does not mean the remaining amount is permanently unrecoverable: the auditor says restitution settlements continue beyond the report, and the programs that administer the benefits are responsible for collection activity. the lag does show why an investigation announcement and a completed recovery are different stages of public accountability. the quarterly split also shows where the total accumulated. in the third quarter of the state's fiscal year, the bureau investigated 994 cases and identified fraud in 168 cases, with overpayments totaling $2,981,696. in the fourth quarter, it investigated 1,229 cases and identified fraud in 234 cases, with overpayments totaling $7,630,886. the report says the fourth-quarter figures include the resumption of referrals through the document benefit fraud task force and two dental-provider cases involving alleged billing for impossible days. the bureau of special investigations operates within the office of the state auditor and can investigate allegations involving programs administered by the department of transitional assistance, the department of children and families and the division of medical assistance, which runs masshealth. its authority does not include collecting settlements or prosecuting cases. those decisions move to the relevant benefit programs and, when appropriate, state or federal prosecutors. boston 25 reported that the executive office of health and human services defended its program-integrity processes while saying agencies had referred most of the cases to the auditor's office. for residents, the report's immediate significance is less about a single statewide bill than about how quickly suspected overpayments are detected, referred and recovered. the auditor's office is asking people with information about possible public-assistance fraud to use its anonymous reporting channels, including the bureau of special investigations hotline at (617) 727-6771. the next measurable steps will be agency decisions on disqualification, civil recoupment or prosecution, along with any future reports showing how much of the identified money is ultimately recovered. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma boston massachusetts massachusetts public benefits fraud investigations masshealth snap state auditor oversight

me-home-heating-costs-neada-2026-10-01.excerpt: A new regional estimate puts the average Maine household's heating-oil cost 77% above last winter, as state data show prices above $6 a gallon and assistance applications open.
me-home-heating-costs-neada-2026-10-01.text: maine oil-heating bills projected to approach $3,000 this winter a new regional estimate puts the average maine household's heating-oil cost 77% above last winter, as state data show prices above $6 a gallon and assistance applications open. maine households that heat with oil are facing a sharply more expensive winter, with the average cost projected to reach $2,939, according to a september 29 report by wmtw news 8 citing the national energy assistance directors association. the estimate is for the 2026-27 heating season and does not represent a guaranteed bill for every household. the projected figure is 77% higher than the $1,664 comparison figure reported for last winter. wmtw said that increase is tied with vermont for the largest projected rise among states in the northeast. the comparison is especially significant in maine, where heating oil remains a major household fuel and where many homes begin the heating season with little room for a large price shock. the estimate arrived as maine's own fuel survey showed oil prices at $6.02 per gallon. the maine department of energy resources reported that statewide average on september 21, with surveyed prices ranging from $5.00 to $6.45. the department cautions that the figures are cash prices from delivered-fuel retailers, not pre-buy or discounted contracts, and that local prices can vary considerably. its current price page is https://www.maine.gov/energy/heating-fuel-prices. a seasonal average is not the same as a forecast for an individual home. actual spending will depend on the amount of oil a household uses, the size and efficiency of the building, the length and severity of the cold season, and the price charged by the local supplier. the projection also describes heating-oil users; households using propane, natural gas, wood or electricity will face different costs. maine's energy office says its comparison dashboard is intended to show relative heating costs and does not include the cost of installing a new heating system. the price pressure matters beyond the monthly fuel bill. a household that spends more to heat its home has less money available for rent, food, transportation and medical expenses. it can also make the timing of a delivery important: a family that delays an order while waiting for a lower price may still need fuel before the weather turns colder. maine's department of energy resources publishes a winter-heating guide and updates its delivered-fuel survey during the heating season, giving consumers a way to compare the statewide benchmark with local offers. state assistance is available for eligible households, but it is income- and household-size based. mainehousing says its home energy assistance program helps qualified homeowners and renters with heating costs, fuel deliveries, energy-related repairs and some utility payments. applications for the 2026-27 heap season opened august 3 and continue until funds are exhausted or may 29, 2027. details and the application are available at https://www.mainehousing.org/programs-services/energy/energydetails/liheap. mainehousing also says crisis assistance for households with extremely low fuel supplies will open november 1. that program requires a heap application first and is administered through local community action agencies. the agency encourages residents to apply early, because benefits depend on eligibility and available funds. for readers trying to plan, the immediate next steps are to check the current local price, review the state's assistance rules and avoid treating the $2,939 projection as a promise that every home will spend the same amount. maine maine maine me augusta maine maine heating oil home heating energy costs mainehousing heap affordability
